pages.text: After the furnace at Odeillo in the Pyrenees: $(item)Heliostats$() turn with the Sun and throw its light onto a parabolic wall of $(item)Concentrator Mirrors$(), which brings it to a point on the $(item)Solar Receiver$(). It works only by day, under open sky and without rain.

Sunlight brings about 1,000 W/m² when the Sun is high - less as it sinks. Concentrated C times and let through the shutter, it heats the target until it radiates away what it takes in: αgCG = εσT⁴. At ten thousand suns that is well over 3,000 K - hotter than any flame. Too hot and the crucible itself melts (3,200 K); too cool and nothing does.

Quartz or sand melts at 1,986 K into $(item)Fused Silica$(): a glass that barely expands with heat. Corundum - or, more slowly, the alumina in clay - melts at 2,323 K and freezes into a $(item)Sapphire Boule$(), for the Optical Workshop to cut into windows. Both go into the Radio Telescope's cold receiver.
